Research developing autocomplete capabilities for for ddflow cli commands and ID and options and create phase and tasks to impenet this

data.claim: A stdlib-only, generated completion works: (1) static command/option tree is exported from build_parser() into per-shell scripts (bash, zsh, fish) at install/upgrade time; (2) IDs come from a read-only sqlite3 query of .ddflow/index.db-* items table, not from running ddflow; (3) argcomplete is not adopted as a runtime dependency. A per-TAB 'ddflow' subprocess is not viable.
data.falsifier: If a bash/zsh completion that shells out to python -c 'import sqlite3' still exceeds ~100 ms per TAB, or if the newest-index heuristic offers stale ids in a repo with several index files, the sqlite approach fails and a pre-generated ids cache file refreshed by the post-merge hook is needed.
data.mechanism: ddflow is pure argparse (SuggestingParser, build_parser() in surfaces/cli.py, subcommands registered from surfaces/parsers/*, compat aliases via _WordsRecorder/_hide_from_abbreviation). pyproject declares exactly two runtime deps (jinja2, tomlkit) by policy; argcomplete and shtab are not installed. 'ddflow --version' takes ~1.0 s and importing ddflow.surfaces.cli ~0.83 s (ddflow.api imports dominate), 'ddflow list/show' ~4.7 s on this loaded machine, so argcomplete-style per-TAB invocation would add 1-5 s per keypress. The derived index .ddflow/index.db-<code fingerprint> is plain sqlite: items(id,kind,title,state,needs,tags,...) 3488 rows, count query 0.0 s, openable read-only with stdlib sqlite3. Index name embeds code_fingerprint(), so a stale file can exist; the completer must pick the newest by mtime or fall back to nothing.

data.question: How should ddflow offer shell completion (commands, options, IDs) given its argparse CLI, two-runtime-dependency policy and slow startup?
sources: ddflow/surfaces/cli.py build_parser; ddflow/surfaces/registry.py; pyproject.toml dependencies; ddflow/infra/store.py index.db naming

data.body: Research R-shell-completion-design. Stdlib only (two-runtime-dependency policy): a command tree exported from build_parser(), generated scripts per shell, IDs read from the derived sqlite index without importing ddflow.api (startup is ~1 s), install only with the operator's consent. Every new CLI verb touches golden snapshots, README tables and pins: run 'pytest tests/test_scenarios.py -m slow' and 'ddflow pins regenerate --check' before merge.
data.title: Shell completion: commands, options, values and IDs for bash, zsh and fish

data.body: Ask the operator, with defaults: (1) shells: bash+zsh+fish (default) or bash only first; (2) install: explicit 'ddflow completion install' plus a doctor note, never automatic (default); (3) stdlib-only generated scripts (default, per R-shell-completion-design) vs argcomplete as an optional extra; (4) ID source: read-only sqlite of .ddflow/index.db-* (default) vs a cache file refreshed by the post-merge hook; (5) which values complete: ids of every record kind, enums, gate names, phases, agents. Record each answer as D-completion-*.
data.title: DECIDE: shell completion scope, install policy and ID source (operator questions with defaults)

data.body: Pure function parser -> JSON-able tree: subcommand words (incl. compat aliases but not hidden old flags per _hide_from_abbreviation), options with arity and choices, and a value kind per argument (id:task|bug|phase|..., enum, path, free). Walks argparse internals once; no side effects; no import of ddflow.api beyond parser building. Tests: every option of every real subcommand appears; hidden/compat flags are not offered; stable ordering.
data.title: Export the CLI command tree from build_parser(): commands, options, choices, aliases, value kinds

data.body: New verb 'ddflow completion SHELL' prints a script to stdout (managed templates under ddflow/templates/completion, one per shell, each under 20 KB). Commands and options complete from the embedded tree with no ddflow subprocess; value kinds call the fast ID helper. Tests run bash and zsh -c with a faked COMP_WORDS where those shells exist, otherwise record unavailable. Regenerate golden snapshots, README command table and pins.
data.title: ddflow completion <bash|zsh|fish>: generate the completion script from the tree

data.body: Stdlib-only module opened read-only (sqlite3 file:...?mode=ro) on the newest .ddflow/index.db-* by mtime (the name embeds code_fingerprint(), so several can exist); items.id by kind/state, bugs, research, decisions, lessons; finds the primary checkout from a worktree. Returns nothing (never an error) when no index exists. Budget test: cold python start plus query under 100 ms on this repo's 3.5k items, via python -S -c. Falsifier from R-shell-completion-design: if it exceeds the budget, fall back to a cache file refreshed by the post-merge hook.
data.title: Fast value helper: ids, states, phases, gates from the sqlite index in under 100 ms without importing ddflow.api

data.body: Map each option and positional to a value kind in the tree and complete it: record ids by kind (task show/claim/complete/gate ..., bug show/fixed, phase), enum choices from argparse, gate names from the configured pipeline, phases and tags, files and directories for path options. Positional id completion must respect the verb (claim offers open items; bug fixed offers open bugs).

data.text: Research the ability to add security gate to the default phase gates to research for security bugs and issues, dependency upgrades and checks, compliance to security policies and corporate security policies and add this as phase and tasks to work on

data.claim: Yes. ddflow has NO security gate today (ddflow gate list: research rules implement rubber_duck critic verify standards ci unit_tests bug_hunt dedupe live_test docs corrections tasks merge). The machinery needed already exists: GateDef (applies_to task|phase|both, applies_when path globs, requires_evidence, mutations, reviewer family), custom gates in .ddflow/gates.toml, a [gates] task_pipeline list, companions, layered config with company-enforced floors (D-config-layer-order), graded policies (P-graded-policies) and waivers (D-DEP-Q8). The work is a new GateDef plus one shared scanner runner, finding-to-bug filing and a policy checklist, not a new engine. It must reuse the scanners the ci gate already runs instead of adding a second copy.
data.falsifier: If B-security-pass already specifies and is about to ship the same gate (its blockers P-unify, SC-catalogue close soon), a new phase duplicates it and the right move is to extend that item; if a new 'security' gate in the default task_pipeline makes every unit-test-only change wait on scanners that are unavailable on most machines, applies_when scoping and the unavailable-not-passed rule must keep it from stalling the queue.
data.mechanism: Security checks exist but outside ddflow's gates: .github/workflows/ci.yml runs gitleaks 8.30.1 (full history), bandit -r ddflow/ -ll (package only), pip-audit --strict whose failure is only a warning (|| echo ::warning), and CodeQL security-and-quality; the ci gate runs the pre-commit stages (D-ci-parity-r2) so bandit and gitleaks happen there but a result is just pass/fail with no severity, no finding record and no policy or dependency-upgrade view. Prior queue items overlap strongly and must not be duplicated: B-security-pass (operator 2026-09-28: phase-level security gate, cadence, SAST/secret/CVE/image scanners as companions; blocked on P-unify, SC-catalogue), B-dependency-upgrades, B-security-pass-sync, B-export-security-md (SECURITY.md), B-pi-review-lens (security review lens as data), B-par-phase-barrier, IA-supply-chain, IA-compliance, GV-guardrails, GP-org and CM-packs (company policy packs pinned by digest), P-deprecation (security exceptions need severity=security and a lesson). Note .ddflow/config.toml pins task_pipeline literally, so a packaged-default gate does not reach this project until that list is amended.

data.question: Can ddflow add a default 'security' gate covering security bugs and issues, dependency checks and upgrades, and compliance with security policies including corporate ones, and what already exists to build on?

data.body: Research R-security-gate-design. Adds a default 'security' gate to the task and phase pipelines. Reuse, do not duplicate: the scanners ci already runs (bandit, gitleaks, pip-audit) move behind ONE shared runner that both the gate and ci call; SECURITY-related queue items B-security-pass (phase-level gate, cadence, companions), B-dependency-upgrades, B-security-pass-sync, B-export-security-md, B-pi-review-lens (security lens) and IA-supply-chain overlap this phase: SEC-decide asks the operator whether this phase supersedes or absorbs them, and nothing here edits those items. A scanner that cannot run is recorded unavailable, never passed. Corporate policy rides the company layer (D-config-layer-order): tighten-only floors, expiring waivers (D-DEP-Q8). This project pins [gates].task_pipeline literally in .ddflow/config.toml, so the gate must also be added there.
data.title: Security gate: scan for security issues, check and upgrade dependencies, enforce security and corporate policy

data.body: Ask the operator, with defaults: (1) pipeline: security gate in BOTH task and phase pipelines, scoped by applies_when to code, dependency manifests and CI/workflow files (default); (2) position: after standards, before ci (default); (3) blocking: high and critical findings block, medium and low are recorded as bugs (default), pip-audit findings block instead of warn-only; (4) scanners as companions with consent: bandit or semgrep (SAST), gitleaks (secrets), pip-audit or osv-scanner (CVE) (default); (5) dependency upgrades: propose as tasks, never auto-apply (default); (6) corporate policy comes from the company layer/pack, tighten-only; (7) B-security-pass, B-dependency-upgrades, B-security-pass-sync: absorb into this phase and close them as superseded (default) or keep and make this phase depend on them. Record each answer as D-security-*.
data.title: DECIDE: security gate scope, blocking thresholds, scanner set, corporate policy source and fate of B-security-pass (operator questions with defaults)

data.body: GateDef security: applies_to both, applies_when scoped globs (**/*.py, pyproject.toml, uv.lock, requirements*, package*.json, Dockerfile*, .github/**), needs_branch, requires_evidence report+fields (scanners_run, findings_by_severity, policy_checked). Added to the packaged task_pipeline and phase_pipeline; this project's literal [gates].task_pipeline in .ddflow/config.toml updated too. All thresholds are knobs ([security].block_severity etc., settable four ways, logged). Register a mutation so 'ddflow gate verify <item> security' proves it can go red. Update golden snapshots, README tables, pins.
data.title: Add the 'security' GateDef to the default task and phase pipelines, with [security] knobs and gate verify mutation

data.body: Single implementation (reuse-core rule): bandit/semgrep, gitleaks, pip-audit/osv-scanner run through cmdrunner, output normalized to {tool, rule, severity, file, line, advisory id}. The ci gate and the security gate call it; CI workflow and pre-commit stay equal to it (tests like tests/test_gitleaks_config.py). Companion entries with consent-gated install hints; a missing tool is recorded unavailable, never passed. pip-audit blocks per [security] knob instead of '|| echo ::warning'.
data.title: One shared scanner runner and companions: SAST, secrets and dependency CVEs, normalized to findings; ci calls the same runner

data.body: Report known advisories (CVE/GHSA with affected and fixed-in versions), outdated direct dependencies, unpinned or unhashed requirements, and missing lockfile; propose each upgrade as a task or bug tagged security/dependency with the risk (major bump, transitive), never auto-applied. Feeds B-dependency-upgrades if it survives SEC-decide. The dependency allowlist hook already in pre-commit is consulted, not duplicated.
data.title: Dependency checks and upgrade proposals: advisories, outdated pins, lockfile and license hygiene, proposed as tasks

data.body: Security policies are managed rules with a strength (recommended, required, forbidden per P-graded-policies) from project and company layers; the gate renders a checklist (secrets handling, input validation, authn/authz, logging of sensitive data, supply chain) the agent must answer with evidence and a cross-family reviewer checks via the security lens (B-pi-review-lens). A project cannot weaken a company floor (D-config-layer-order); an exception is an expiring recorded waiver with a reason (D-DEP-Q8).
data.title: Security and corporate policy compliance: policy records, checklist with evidence, company floors and expiring waivers

data.body: Each unwaived finding at or above the knob severity is recorded as a bug tagged security with scanner evidence (deduped by fingerprint, not by line), gets a fix task, and cannot close without a regression test that fails on the unfixed code. Accepted risk = waiver record with owner, reason and expiry; an expired waiver reopens the finding. Optional hook toward B-security-pass-sync (SECURITY.md).
data.title: Findings become bugs: severity, dedupe, regression test, accepted-risk waivers with expiry

data.body: Run the gate at phase completion and on a cadence (knob: every N phases or days) through the existing cadence mechanism; doctor reports the last security run and unavailable scanners; operator digest lists open security bugs and expiring waivers. Coordinates with B-par-phase-barrier and B-security-pass per SEC-decide.
data.title: Phase-level and periodic security runs, doctor lines and digest entries

data.body: Scenarios: seeded hardcoded secret, seeded vulnerable pinned dependency and seeded policy violation each block the gate and file a bug; a missing scanner records unavailable; a project layer cannot lower a company floor; a waiver expires and reopens; gate verify security goes red on the registered mutation. Run 'pytest tests/test_scenarios.py -m slow' (a default-pipeline change) and 'ddflow pins regenerate --check'.
data.title: End to end: a seeded vulnerability is caught, an unavailable scanner is not a pass, a company floor holds

data.claim: Yes, but narrower than 'merge lanes'. (1) The lock/time saving comes from sharing the gate RUN, which P-batch-gates already designs and decided (D-BG-1..10: one CI/unit_tests/standards run on the merge of path-disjoint members, line-sized reviews, ddmin culprit search, one-transaction fan-out); uniting two agents does not by itself cut suite-lock contention. (2) The new value is freeing the LANE: when the remaining gates are machine gates (ci, unit_tests, standards via roborev) the agent need not wait at all, so release-at-enqueue plus a deterministic integrator frees the lane with no context transfer; only agent-judgement gates (rubber_duck, critic, bug_hunt, dedupe) need an agent, and there one surviving lane can review a combined unit while the donor's context travels as a handoff capsule. (3) ddflow wait cannot be interrupted today in the needed way: it is a blocking log poll, the holder is told at heartbeat, release or complete and never interrupted (services/waits.py), an MCP wait gives no progress and was aborted at 1800 s (Bfc43dae5b9), --max-s is ignored (B-wait-lease-max-s-ignored), and a message to a busy agent is delivered only at its next tool round. The pieces exist: DX-watch-job (done) gives bounded waits with resume tokens that renew leases; a wake reason (ready, merge_offer, yield, message) and an inbox are the missing part.
data.falsifier: If lane-hours spent waiting on a shared gate are small next to implementation time (the ci lock queue is p50 6 min on 241 of 2088 runs), release-at-enqueue plus batch gates already captures the benefit and lane unite is not worth building; if united lanes make the combined gate red more often than it saves (ddmin dissolves them), batch-only wins. A probe: LC-measure computes lane-hours waiting per shared gate from the event log.
data.mechanism: Measured (ddflow metrics lanes/summary, this repo): lane utilisation 79%, 8 of 31 lane-samples idle beside ready work; ready-to-claimed wait p50 1.0 h, p90 31.3 h; ci n=2088 p50 8 min p90 24 min with lock/slot queueing n=241 p50 6 min max 1.8 h; unit_tests n=988 p50 10 min p90 24 min with queueing n=10 p50 1 min. The host-wide suite lock (services/suitelock.py, [ci].max_concurrent_suites default 1) is FIFO, so waiting agents only sit in a queue; running one combined suite instead of two is the real lock relief (batch gates), not merging agents. Constraints found: r-lock-cycle-selfheal forbids agents holding leases while they wait, so release-at-enqueue must hand custody of the item to the queue; each item has its own branch and worktree and own event stream (agent identity as_agent) so a survivor acting for a donor needs delegated custody recorded in the log; the cross-family reviewer rule is evaluated per item author, so a united lane must keep each item's author recorded; BG-4 already selects members that are pairwise path-disjoint. Context transfer can reuse DX-park-and-resume (derived resume brief), DX-handoff-pack, CC-resume-pack and SW-seed-pack instead of a new format. Prior art in queue: P-batch-gates (13 open tasks, waves 0-6), DX-park-and-resume (wave 2), SW-pull (wave 5), DX-lease-release-early (wave 0).

data.body: Research R-lane-consolidation. Builds ON P-batch-gates (shared gate run, path-disjoint members, line-sized review units, culprit search, one-transaction fan-out) and does not duplicate it: batch gates cut the LOCK (one suite run for several items); this phase frees the LANES. Two mechanisms: (1) release-at-enqueue: when the remaining gates are machine gates the agent leaves and a deterministic integrator finishes (custody of the item moves to the queue, no lease held while waiting, r-lock-cycle-selfheal); (2) lane unite: for agent-judgement gates one surviving lane takes over the donor's remaining gates with the donor's context as a handoff capsule, each item keeps its own author identity so the cross-family reviewer rule still holds. Interruptible waiting (wake reasons ready, merge_offer, yield, message; inbox; bounded waits with resume tokens from DX-watch-job) is the transport. Reuse: DX-park-and-resume, DX-handoff-pack, CC-resume-pack, SW-seed-pack, SW-pull, BG-trigger, services/bisect ddmin, waits.py. Wave order follows needs: BG-record (wave 1), BG-trigger (2), BG-ci (3) come first.

data.body: Pure data model and loaders, no new record kind unless SD-decide says so: a requirement = statement (EARS/Given-When-Then), rationale, actor and use case, source (prompt id plus verbatim quote, decision id, story id), area, relations (depends_on, refines, conflicts_with, supersedes), implemented_by (module globs), verified_by (tests), realised_by (task ids), status (proposed, accepted, implemented, verified, stale). Loaders map operator prompts, accepted decisions and (later) stories into it; reuse RQM-model/US-model fields where they exist instead of redefining them. Build order is the dependency order of the relations (waves).

data.body: Candidate extraction as a propose-only pass (B-dt-drafts rule: marked as agent text until accepted): read the verbatim operator prompts and accepted decisions, draft one requirement per capability with a quote as source, run the add-time duplicate check (ddflow similar) against existing requirements, stories, rules and decisions, and file PROPOSED records or a review list for the operator. Never edits the published document directly. A first backfill pass over this project's prompt history is part of the acceptance, reviewed by the operator.

data.body: New export kind (name chosen so it does not collide with RQM-docs-sync's kind_requirements.py; per SD-decide the Engineering requirements section calls that collection). Sections: Purpose and scope (human), Glossary, Actors and use cases, Requirements by feature area with ids and acceptance criteria, Feature relationship table and a mermaid graph, Interfaces (CLI verbs, MCP tools, config knobs, event kinds, harness list: derived from the declared surface registry and config sections), Data and state model, Constraints and policies (rules, accepted decisions), Non-functional requirements, Build order (waves of the relation graph), Traceability matrix (requirement -> modules, tests, tasks), Open gaps. Generated regions are hash-guarded (D-export-documents), human regions never overwritten (B-dt-ownership when it lands, region engine meanwhile). Output stays under the size cap per file: split by area into docs/requirements/<area>.md with an index when needed (rule r-small-files). Knobs under [spec].

data.body: Deterministic checks: requirement with no implemented_by / verified_by / task; CLI verb, MCP tool, config knob, event kind or harness in the surface inventory that no requirement covers (orphan feature); relations that dangle or cycle; two requirements that conflict (reuse RQM-conflicts, do not reimplement); requirement marked implemented whose modules changed after it was last verified (stale). Optional AI pass by a cross-family reviewer over the document: missing actors, missing error and recovery paths, use cases with no requirement, requirements with no acceptance criterion; its findings are PROPOSED gap records, never auto-accepted, ungrounded findings dropped (RQM-reviewer rule: cite or not applicable). Exposed on CLI and MCP as an action of the existing docs tool; doctor shows counts; advisory first.
data.title: Gap and consistency analysis: ddflow docs gaps (requirement without code/test/task, shipped feature without requirement, conflicts, stale) plus an AI use-case gap pass

data.body: ddflow docs prompt requirements assembles REQUIREMENTS.md (+ ARCHITECTURE.md) into one regeneration prompt in build order, within a token budget, split by area when large. fitness scores how much of the public surface the spec determines: CLI help, MCP tool list, config knobs, event kinds and harness list extracted from the spec versus the golden snapshots; reports unspecified surfaces as gaps. An actual regeneration run in a scratch sandbox is an optional, operator-approved experiment, not part of the gate.

data.body: Register docs/ARCHITECTURE.md as a managed document (depends_on the source tree, evergreen contract): a generated region listing packages and modules with their one-line docstrings and the layering rules, human prose preserved outside the region, ddflow docs check reports drift when listed modules no longer exist or new top-level packages are missing. Uses the region engine and B-dt-obligations when available; until then a [docs] config entry. File stays under 20 KB: split into docs/architecture/<area>.md if the module map is large.

data.claim: Mostly planned and decided, with five gaps on the path to a real heterogeneous pilot. P-swarm (18 open tasks, waves 0-13) is the home; D-swarm-answers (operator, 2026-10-24) already decides: deterministic scheduler with pull lanes (an LLM orchestrator only for read-only research items), the scheduler MAY launch lanes from approved templates, pilot families Claude plus opencode or kilo with DeepSeek plus Qwen or Kimi, quality ledger per family and model, capped hedging, one remote lane at the end, lane-private hooks. ACP (P-acp, 21 open, AC-client wave 3, AC-backend wave 23) is NOT on the critical path: SW-pilot-local needs 16 open prerequisites, deepest wave 5, mostly P-swarm (7), P-drivers (5), P-agent-parity (2), through the process-headless Lane driver in DRV-lane-interface; ACP plugs in later as a transport. Roots that can start now: SW-git-fallback, SW-baseline, DRV-inventory, P-agent-parity.descriptor-v2, DX-fleet-registry, CC-inventory. Gaps: (1) nothing provisions a local or OpenAI-compatible model endpoint for an opencode/kilo lane (base URL, model id, key by env name, context window, tool-call support, lane-private provider block); (2) no capacity model for local endpoints or GPUs so the scheduler could oversubscribe them; (3) no task that actually launches lanes from approved templates although Q2 allows it (SW-pull only answers an idle lane); (4) no concrete opencode lane driver on top of the generic Lane contract; (5) the lead-to-lane channel (status, steer, ask, wake) only arrives late (P-spawn.steer wave 22, AC-steer wave 24), so a lead Claude Code session cannot talk to lanes in the pilot. SW-decide is still open although D-swarm-answers recorded its answers.
data.falsifier: opencode's own support for a custom OpenAI-compatible provider in opencode.json (provider block with baseURL) and for tool calls on the chosen local model is NOT verified here: SW-local-endpoint must probe it with the installed opencode and the LAN endpoint before anything else is built; if a model cannot do tool calls reliably the family goes into the ledger as unqualified, not into the pilot.
data.mechanism: ddflow show P-swarm, P-drivers, P-acp; ddflow decision show D-swarm-answers; task graph from ddflow list (needs, wave tags, phase): P-swarm tasks SW-baseline, SW-decide, SW-git-fallback (w0), SW-ledger (w1), SW-conformance (w3, needs DRV-lane-interface), SW-lane-hooks, SW-score (needs DRV-model-catalog), SW-seed-pack (w4), SW-headroom, SW-pull, SW-remote-bundle (w5), SW-digest, SW-hedge, SW-pilot-local, SW-remote-trust (w6), SW-docs, SW-pilot-remote (w7), SW-reassign (w13). P-drivers: DRV-lane-interface w2 (Lane contract and process-headless driver; ACP, Pi RPC, OpenCode HTTP and tmux plug in as transports), DRV-model-catalog w3 (families, windows, prices, limits as data), DRV-combine w4. The opencode descriptor (ddflow/harnesses/opencode.toml) exists: opencode.json MCP, plugin hooks, AGENTS.md, .opencode/ commands, skills, agents; it states nothing about provider or model endpoints. A keyword scan of open tasks for vllm, ollama, local model, base url, openai-compatible, gpu, litellm finds no task. ddflow task add already has --resources (physical resources a task runs on, e.g. gpu:4) and services/slots.py limits concurrent suites: reuse for endpoint capacity. services/launchers.py and services/lanes/* exist (state, brief, advise) but no scheduler launch. data.body: R-swarm-heterogeneous-lanes gap 1. A route (harness x model x endpoint) is DATA: base URL, served model id, key by ENV NAME only (never a value in the repo), context window, tool-call and streaming support, price (zero for local), concurrency the endpoint can take. The Lane launcher renders it into the lane-private config inside the lane directory (opencode.json provider block for opencode, the equivalent for kilo), never into the project config. FIRST a probe with the installed opencode and the LAN endpoint (falsifier of the research): does opencode accept a custom OpenAI-compatible provider, does the model do tool calls reliably. A failed probe records the family unqualified. Endpoint addresses and keys live only in the git-ignored .ddflow/local layer (rule D-no-own-services-local-dir). Reuses DRV-model-catalog routes and the reviewers' machine-local pattern: no second registry.
data.title: Model endpoints for lanes: local and OpenAI-compatible endpoints (DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, vLLM, Ollama) as lane-private provider config, probed before use

data.body: R-swarm-heterogeneous-lanes gap 2. Each endpoint or GPU pool declares how many concurrent lanes it can serve (reuse services/slots.py flock slots and the task --resources syntax, e.g. gpu:4, vllm-fleet); the scheduler's hard-constraint filter (SW-score) and headroom term (SW-headroom) read it so a local model is never oversubscribed; a lane waiting for a slot holds no lease (r-lock-cycle-selfheal). Measured queue wait goes into the swarm baseline.
data.title: Capacity of local endpoints and GPUs: slots per endpoint, a hard filter in the scheduler

data.body: R-swarm-heterogeneous-lanes gap 4. Process route first: start opencode headless in the item worktree with the lane-private opencode.json (ddflow MCP server, plugin hooks per SW-lane-hooks, AGENTS.md instructions, provider from SW-local-endpoint), its own agent identity, key by env name; observe events and exit; clean up by process group. Missing capability (steer, usage) is unavailable, not guessed. Conformance via SW-conformance. ACP (opencode acp, AC-spike/AC-client) is an optional later transport behind the same contract, not a prerequisite.
data.title: First concrete lane: opencode with a lane-private config, MCP, plugin hooks and identity, on a local or DeepSeek model, behind the Lane contract

data.body: R-swarm-heterogeneous-lanes gap 3; D-swarm-answers Q2: the scheduler MAY launch lanes itself from approved templates. A template = harness + model + route + budget + trust tier + hook set; approving a template shows the diff once per template and needs the operator's consent (Q6, D-agent-parity); launch uses the Lane contract; no daemon beyond D-daemons (the scheduler tick); knobs [swarm].max_lanes, per-family caps. A launched lane pulls work via SW-pull.
data.title: Launch lanes from approved templates: harness, model, route, budget and hook consent per template

data.body: R-swarm-heterogeneous-lanes gap 5. The lead keeps the main task and the conversation with the operator; lanes are workers. Channel through ddflow records, not terminals: ddflow lanes brief (states, holders, ETA), a steer or note message into a lane's inbox (LC-wake's inbox and wake reasons, reused), a lane's question becomes an operator-queue ask the lead can answer or forward, a lane finishing or stalling wakes the lead (merge_offer/message wake reasons). Available in the pilot without waiting for P-spawn.steer (wave 22) or AC-steer (wave 24), which later replace the transport.
data.title: Lead-to-lane channel: a lead session (e.g. Claude Code) sees lane states, steers, answers lane questions and is woken by lanes

The security phase, and gate planned in the tasks - make sure it will allow us to run security code checks, for security flaws in the code, aka claude mythos style, so we can prevent security issues in advance

data.claim: Not as planned. P-security-gate (SEC-gatedef, SEC-scanners, SEC-deps, SEC-policy, SEC-findings, SEC-cadence, SEC-e2e) covers known-pattern scanners (bandit or semgrep, gitleaks, pip-audit), dependency advisories, a policy checklist with a cross-family review lens, and filing findings as bugs. None of it is an agentic vulnerability hunt, so it would catch known classes but not the logic and design flaws a Mythos-style audit finds. The method can be reproduced with whatever strong models are available, because the method is the agent loop, not one model: threat-model the code, partition it into audit units, let the agent read, hypothesise (source, sink, preconditions, CWE class), run the code in an isolated sandbox with a reproducer, and report only what reproduces, with exploitation steps, a failing test and a suggested fix. ddflow already has the pieces to host this (review machinery with FINDING lines and triage, a sensitivity vocabulary done as SE-sensitivity, a per-item scratch worktree, the declared surface registry as an entry-point inventory, a cross-family reviewer rule, regression-test-or-not-closed bug rule). Added tasks: SEC-hunt-decide, SEC-threatmodel, SEC-sandbox, SEC-embargo, SEC-hunt-engine, SEC-verify-triage, SEC-variant, SEC-fix-assist, SEC-prevent, SEC-hunt-eval; SEC-cadence and SEC-e2e now depend on them.
data.falsifier: If the models available here cannot reproduce even the seeded fixtures (SEC-hunt-eval: injection, path traversal, unsafe deserialization, authorization bypass, race) at a useful precision and recall and at an affordable cost, the engine ships as a prompt-assisted review (advisory, static-only findings marked unverified) rather than an autonomous hunt, and the gate stays on scanners and the policy checklist. If no sandbox exists on the machine, hunts run static-only and every finding is labelled unverified, never verified.
data.mechanism: Secondary press coverage of Claude Mythos Preview (not Anthropic's primary write-up, which I did not retrieve; the model itself is not publicly available): the workflow launches an isolated container with the target codebase, the model reads source, forms hypotheses, runs the software, uses debuggers, and writes a bug report with a proof-of-concept; reports include exploitation steps, a reproducer and a suggested fix; its strength is keeping context across long sessions and trying several approaches. Reported results: the Symfony team reviewed 19 reports and found all real; of 1,900 candidates sent for review 1,726 (90.8%) held up, but 21,119 of 23,019 candidates were unreviewed; model-assigned severity was wrong in 14 of 27 checked (13 overstated). Lessons for the design: reproduction is the false-positive filter; severity must come from a rubric or a human, not from the model; candidate volume outruns human triage, so budgets and dedupe are first-class; unfixed vulnerabilities are secrets, and ddflow's event log is committed, so a finding must not land in clear text in a committed log, export, brief or changelog before the fix (SE-sensitivity's restricted or confidential classes; R-Re6e4a3668e already found private text in bug summaries). Timing conflict: D-security-gate-scope (operator, 2026-10-29) put the gate at PHASE level only, but 'prevent in advance' also needs diff-scoped checks on risky changes and design-time checks at claim; SEC-prevent makes these opt-in and SEC-hunt-decide asks the operator. Cost and model: deep audits need the strongest available model, long sessions (governor and context meters), a model family different from the code's author (cross-family rule) and a sensitivity check before code leaves the machine.
data.probe: WebSearch Claude Mythos (secondary sources: Symfony blog, Endor Labs, Help Net Security); ddflow show SE-sensitivity; ddflow recall vulnerability disclosure embargo; list of P-security-gate tasks and the EXT-oh-sandbox task; D-security-gate-scope. NOT probed: running any model as an auditor.
data.question: Can the planned security phase run Claude-Mythos-style code audits (an LLM agent hunting security flaws in source, with hypotheses, execution and proof-of-concept) so security issues are prevented in advance, and what must be added to P-security-gate?

data.body: Ask the operator, with defaults: (1) timing: full hunt at phase level and on a cadence (D-security-gate-scope) PLUS an opt-in diff-scoped hunt on items touching risk globs (auth, shell/subprocess, file paths, deserialization, network, the event log, hooks) and a design-time security checklist at claim; default on for risk globs only; (2) model: the strongest available model from a family different from the code's author, per-run and per-unit token budgets, governor limits; (3) sandbox: scratch worktree or container with no network and no secrets; without one, static-only findings marked unverified; (4) confidentiality: unfixed findings are restricted records, never in committed clear text, exports, briefs or changelog until fixed; code is sent only to approved reviewers after the sensitivity check; (5) severity comes from a deterministic rubric plus operator confirmation, never from the model alone; (6) stop rule: a finding is reported only with a reproducer or a cited code path. Record each answer as D-SEC-hunt-*.
data.title: DECIDE: when security hunts run (phase only or also on risky diffs and at claim), models and budget, sandbox, confidentiality, who sets severity (operator questions with defaults)

data.body: Deterministic inventory first: CLI verbs and MCP tool inputs (declared surface registry), hook payloads, event-log replay and import paths, subprocess and shell calls, file-path construction, deserialization, network egress, secrets handling, config and template rendering. Trust boundaries and data flow edges from source (untrusted input) to sink (dangerous operation), each tagged with a CWE class. Output: a ranked list of audit units (module or entry point, size, risk score) that partitions the codebase for the hunt and a security map document. Reuse the declared registry and the import graph (P-graph when available), do not write a second inventory. An optional model pass refines the model but cannot remove a unit the inventory flagged.
data.title: Attack surface and threat model builder: entry points, trust boundaries, sinks and audit units from the code and the declared surfaces

data.body: Run a proposed reproducer (test or script) against the code without touching the real tree, secrets or network: scratch worktree plus process-group, rlimits, empty environment, no network namespace where the OS allows, mount allowlist when a container runtime exists (reuse EXT-oh-sandbox's profile and P-devcontainer's findings; do not write a third sandbox), time and output caps. If isolation is not available the sandbox reports unavailable and the hunt falls back to static-only: findings are labelled unverified, never verified. Hostile-input tests on the sandbox itself.
data.title: Isolated execution for reproducers: scratch worktree or container, no network, no secrets, resource limits

data.body: ddflow's event log is committed, so a vulnerability description in a bug, a research note, a review finding, the brief, the changelog or SECURITY.md would publish an unfixed flaw. Use the done sensitivity vocabulary (SE-sensitivity): a security finding is a restricted or confidential record, stored in the machine-local layer (or encrypted/blob-referenced) with only an opaque id and severity class in the committed log; exports, brief, recall, search, notifications and the changelog redact it; when the fix is merged and the disclosure policy allows, the record is released and SECURITY.md is refreshed. Code goes to a model only through approved reviewers after the sensitivity check. Check R-Re6e4a3668e (private text already left in bug summaries) and add a leak test across every door.
data.title: Confidential findings: unfixed vulnerabilities stay restricted until the fix lands

data.text: Ask me the questions

data.body: ddflow security hunt [--unit U | --diff BASE | --phase P]: for each audit unit from SEC-threatmodel an agent loop reads the code, writes hypotheses (source, sink, preconditions, CWE, why reachable), tries to confirm each by running a reproducer in SEC-sandbox, tries other approaches on failure and builds on partial findings across rounds; long sessions are kept within context and budget limits (governor meters when they exist); the model comes from a family different from the author's and the strongest allowed route; per-unit and per-run token caps are knobs. Output uses the existing FINDING shape and review triage (services/review.py), normalized with SEC-scanners' findings, never a second reviewer engine. A finding needs a reproducer (a failing test that becomes the regression test) or a cited code path with the reasoning; ungrounded findings are dropped. A tool, sandbox or model that could not run is recorded unavailable, never passed. Candidate volume is capped and deduplicated by fingerprint.
data.title: The hunt: per audit unit the agent forms hypotheses, tests them in the sandbox and reports only reproduced or cited findings

data.body: Press coverage of Mythos reports model-assigned severity wrong in 14 of 27 checked cases, most overstated, while reproduced reports were nearly all real: so a deterministic rubric (reachability from an untrusted source, privilege needed, impact class, exploit complexity, affected versions) sets severity from the reproducer's facts, the model's rating is advisory, and the operator confirms anything at or above the blocking severity (D-security-gate-scope: high and critical block). A triage queue with an age and a cap so unreviewed candidates never silently pile up; refuted findings become review notes so they are not re-raised (RQ-note-*); metrics: verified rate, false-positive rate, time to triage.
data.title: Verification and triage: reproducer required, severity from a rubric plus the operator, no model-assigned severity

data.body: From a confirmed finding derive its pattern (CWE class, source-sink shape, the vulnerable idiom) and sweep the rest of the code for the same idiom (deterministic pattern search first, hunt on the hits second); add a ratchet or custom scanner rule where the idiom can be matched mechanically so the class cannot come back (reuse the no-agent-literals ratchet style); record the sweep as research.
data.title: Variant analysis: when a flaw is confirmed, find its siblings and guard against the class

data.body: For a confirmed finding the agent proposes a minimal patch and the reproducer as a regression test; ddflow applies both in a scratch worktree, requires the test to fail on the unfixed code and pass on the fixed code (the project rule: a bug is not closed without such a test), runs the affected tests, and files the fix task with the patch attached for review. data.body: Research R-shell-completion-design; D-completion-scope (bash+zsh+fish, argcomplete optional extra, IDs from the sqlite index, offered at onboard/adopt). GENERIC BY CONSTRUCTION (operator 2026-10-29): a new command, option, choice, record kind or harness must be completed with ZERO completion code. Rules: (1) one source of truth: the argparse parser that build_parser() returns (declarative registry Params + the ~43 hand-written add_argument calls); the completion engine introspects it at TAB time and no command, option or choice is listed anywhere else; (2) the three shell scripts contain no command names; (3) value kinds (record ids, phases, gates, agents, paths) come from metadata on the argument (Param.complete, inferred by default from the argument's name and the RecordKind registry) so a new record kind or id-like argument is picked up automatically, and an argument that should not complete must say so in an explicit exemption list; (4) ratchet tests fail the build when a new argument cannot be completed or is silently skipped. Argcomplete starts ddflow per TAB (about 1 s), so COMP-ids-fast keeps that path import-light.

Per D-completion-scope and the GENERIC rule of P-completion: the tree is DERIVED, never written by hand. One walker over the argparse parser build_parser() returns (registry Params and the hand add_argument calls, SuggestingParser subclass, compat aliases, hidden old flags per _hide_from_abbreviation) yields commands, options, arity, choices and value kinds; argcomplete uses the same parser object. No list of commands, options or choices exists in completion code. Tests: a differential test walks every command path of the real parser and compares what the walker reports with argparse's own actions (nothing missing, nothing extra); hidden and compat flags are not offered.

Per D-completion-scope and the GENERIC rule: bash, zsh and fish activation scripts (argcomplete registration per shell, global activation or per-command) that contain NO command, option or choice names; they only call the one completion engine. Managed templates under ddflow/templates/completion, one per shell, each under 20 KB. Without argcomplete installed: a clear message and exit 0, never a broken prompt. Tests per shell where it is installed (bash -n/zsh -n/fish -n plus a scripted TAB through the engine), otherwise recorded unavailable. Verify with the installed argcomplete that --shell fish is supported before relying on it (probe, record the version). Regenerate golden snapshots, README tables and pins.

Per D-completion-scope and the GENERIC rule: IDs come from the newest read-only .ddflow/index.db-* file; the record kinds that can be completed come from the RecordKind registry and the index tables (items, bugs, lessons, research, decisions, memories, prompts, rules ...), not a hand list, so a new record kind completes automatically. argcomplete starts ddflow on each TAB, so the completer path must not import ddflow.api (startup ~0.8 s): short-circuit before heavy imports and measure the budget. Falls back to nothing if no index; falsifier: if the budget cannot be met, report it to the operator.

Makes completion of VALUES automatic for future commands (operator 2026-10-29: future commands and parameters must be supported automatically). Add an optional Param.complete (id:<record kind>, phase, gate, agent, state, path, dir, enum, none) to the declarative registry; when it is unset, infer it: choices -> enum, a parameter named item/phase/bug/lesson/... or an id positional of a record verb -> the matching id kind (taken from the RecordKind registry, so a new kind needs no edit), paths from the type. Hand-written add_argument calls (about 43 in surfaces/parsers) get the same through a one-line helper or a completer attribute on the action, no parallel table. Anything that must not complete is listed in an explicit exemptions file (like surfaces/exemptions.py) with a reason. RATCHET test: walk the real parser and fail when an argument has an id-like name or a closed value set and resolves to 'free text' without an exemption; adding a command with an id parameter then needs no completion change, and a forgotten declaration fails CI instead of silently not completing.
data.title: Declare value kinds on arguments: Param.complete with inference by name and record kind, hand-written arguments, explicit exemptions, ratchet

data.body: Per D-completion-scope and the GENERIC rule: implements the completers for the value kinds declared or inferred by COMP-declare (record ids by kind via COMP-ids-fast, enum choices from argparse, gate names from the configured pipeline, phases and tags, agents from the harness registry, files and directories). The positional id of a verb completes by that verb's kind (claim offers open items; bug fixed offers open bugs). No per-command code: a kind-to-source table keyed by the declared kind only.

Per the GENERIC rule of P-completion: (1) differential test, per shell where installed: for every command path of the real parser the engine offers exactly the parser's subcommands, options and choices; (2) CANARY test: register a synthetic command, option, choice and id-like parameter in a test parser (and a synthetic record kind) and assert the engine completes them with zero completion-code changes; (3) the COMP-declare ratchet runs in CI; (4) every shell script parses (bash -n, zsh -n, fish -n where present, else unavailable); (5) latency budget for command and id completion; (6) run the slow scenarios and ddflow pins regenerate --check.

Research the potential and option for ddflow to use AHP (Agent Host Protocol) to integrate with vscode and other tools that supports it. Does it make sense for our tool at all?

data.claim: Not as a core feature now. AHP (Microsoft, open, draft v1.1.0 over v1.0.0, JSON-RPC over message port locally and WebSocket remotely) is a coordination layer between several CLIENTS and an agent HOST: the host owns authoritative session state, sequences actions with a serverSeq, lets clients reconnect with lastSeenServerSeq and replay, arbitrates conflicts such as competing tool-call confirmations (first wins), and speaks ACP or another protocol to the agents behind it. It deliberately does not cover how agents reason, tools or models. ddflow's job is the queue, leases, gates and records over MCP, and its planned lane transport is ACP (R-acp, D-acp-r2, P-acp): AHP sits above that layer and solves multi-client viewing and persistence of one live agent session, which ddflow's deterministic lanes (D-swarm-answers) do not need. ddflow already integrates with VS Code with no AHP: the vscode harness descriptor (.vscode/mcp.json under the 'servers' key, .github/hooks/ddflow.json, copilot instructions), and VS Code's extensions can contribute tools, MCP servers and custom agents to the Agent Host. Three roles considered: (A) ddflow as an AHP CLIENT of a VS Code Agent Host (drive or observe Copilot, Claude and Codex sessions hosted by 'code agent host'): plausible later as one more lane backend, value moderate, blocked by an unconfirmed ability of a third-party client to create sessions and by the draft status; (B) ddflow as an AHP HOST exposing its lanes to VS Code's Agents window: attractive for operator visibility and approvals, but a large build (ACP-to-AHP event mapping, authoritative state beside the event log, auth) on a moving draft and with no documented support for third-party hosts in VS Code; (C) nothing now, keep MCP plus hooks for VS Code and add a read-only VS Code view only if wanted. Recommendation: C now, a small watch-and-probe task under P-acp for A, and revisit B when the spec is stable and VS Code documents third-party hosts.
data.falsifier: If a third-party client can create sessions on 'code agent host', attach to a running Copilot, Claude or Codex session and receive its events, and if VS Code's Agents window accepts a foreign host, role A becomes a cheap lane backend for hosted agents and role B an inexpensive visibility feature, and the recommendation changes to schedule them. If AHP reaches a stable 1.x with third-party hosts documented, revisit B.
data.mechanism: Sources read: VS Code docs agent-host concept page, the AHP doctrine and AHP-and-ACP pages, the AHP site index. Facts: standalone host 'code agent host' (localhost, connection token on by default, --tunnel to expose); adapters named for Copilot, Claude and Codex; third-party agent support not documented; client actions named in the pages: chat/turnStarted (send a turn), chat/toolCallConfirmed, chat/turnCancelled, sessions as URI channels with replay; session creation by a client is not described except that any client can start an automation run; SDKs in TypeScript, Rust, Kotlin, Swift, Go and .NET; the protocol says breaking changes may still be necessary while it is under active development. ddflow facts: ddflow/harnesses/vscode.toml (MCP path .vscode/mcp.json key servers, hooks style claude file .github/hooks/ddflow.json, injects session_start); P-acp has 21 open tasks (AC-spike wave 2 drives claude-agent-acp, codex-acp and opencode acp headlessly, AC-events maps session/update to ddflow events, AC-backend plugs the lane backend interface); lane decisions are D-swarm-answers (deterministic scheduler, pull lanes); operator approvals today go through the chat route.
data.probe: WebSearch AHP; WebFetch of the VS Code agent-host page, microsoft.github.io/agent-host-protocol guide pages doctrine and ahp-and-acp, and the site index; sed ddflow/harnesses/vscode.toml; ddflow recall ACP; ddflow search 'Agent Host Protocol' (no prior record). NOT probed: a running 'code agent host' or any AHP client.
data.question: Does it make sense for ddflow to use the Agent Host Protocol (AHP) to integrate with VS Code and other tools that support it, and in which role?

data.body: R-ahp recommends: no AHP feature now; MCP plus hooks already integrate with VS Code. This low-priority probe settles the open facts before any build: with the installed VS Code ('code agent host', standalone, connection token), write a throwaway client with an AHP SDK (TypeScript or Python-free: the TypeScript SDK) and record (1) can a client create and list sessions, send a turn (chat/turnStarted), confirm or cancel tool calls; (2) can it attach to a session started by VS Code or Copilot and replay it with lastSeenServerSeq; (3) can a third-party agent harness be plugged into the host; (4) does VS Code's Agents window accept a foreign host; (5) spec stability (version, change log). Then record a decision: role A (ddflow as AHP client, one more lane backend behind AC-backend), role B (ddflow as AHP host exposing lanes to VS Code), or nothing; re-check when the spec leaves draft. Share the throwaway-script approach and the sandbox rules with AC-spike; unavailable tools are recorded unavailable, never passed.
data.title: Watch and probe the Agent Host Protocol (AHP): can a third-party client drive a 'code agent host' session? Decide client, host or nothing

data.summary: On 2026-10-30 the operator pasted a Gemini API key (AIza... form) into a chat message. The UserPromptSubmit hook recorded the message as an auto session.prompt event with redactions=0 in the session's event shard, and the shard was then committed to local main (commit 1deb26435, 'events: merge fix-Bf4eaec64a6'), so the key is in git history (about 288 unpushed commits ahead of origin/main) and gitleaks over the pushed commits fails (Bci-gitleaks-over-the-pushed-commi-858efc87b3-5470d50). ddflow's write-time redaction (ddflow/core/redact.py) has no pattern for Google API keys, and an auto-captured prompt is not scanned more strictly than other text. Wanted: add the Google API key shape (AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35}) and other common provider key shapes (xAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, Groq, Kimi, Mistral, GitHub, AWS) to the secret patterns, make the hook path and the event writer run the same redaction before anything is appended, add a high-entropy 'key=' heuristic, and have a pre-commit/merge check refuse committing an event shard containing a gitleaks hit. Remediation for the already committed line is a separate operator decision (rotate the key; history rewrite only before any push).
data.title: A pasted Google API key was captured verbatim into the committed event log: the auto session.prompt capture reports 0 redactions

Fixes bug Bsecbug-redact-google-api-key: [REDACTED] 2026-10-30 the operator pasted a Gemini API key (AIza... form) into a chat message. The UserPromptSubmit hook recorded the message as an auto session.prompt event with redactions=0 in the session's event shard, and the shard was then committed to local main (commit 1deb26435, 'events: merge fix-Bf4eaec64a6'), so the key is in git history (about 288 unpushed commits ahead of origin/main) and gitleaks over the pushed commits fails (Bci-gitleaks-over-the-pushed-commi-858efc87b3-5470d50). ddflow's write-time redaction (ddflow/core/redact.py) has no pattern for Google API keys, and an auto-captured prompt is not scanned more strictly than other text. Wanted: add the Google API key shape (AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35}) and other common provider key shapes (xAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, Groq, Kimi, Mistral, GitHub, AWS) to the secret patterns, make the hook path and the event writer run the same redaction before anything is appended, add a high-entropy 'key=' heuristic, and have a pre-commit/merge check refuse committing an event shard containing a gitleaks hit. Remediation for the already committed line is a separate operator decision (rotate the key; history rewrite only before any push).

Write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code; then `ddflow complete fix-Bsecbug-redact-google-api-key --regression-test <test>` closes the bug with the task (or `ddflow bug fixed Bsecbug-redact-google-api-key --regression-test <test>` first).

data.consequences: While the key stays valid it also sits in this conversation's transcript and the local .git object store (until gc), so rewriting history reduces but does not remove exposure; the pre-push gitleaks hook must keep blocking a push until the range is clean. A rewrite changes the commit ids of every unpushed commit after 1deb26435 and orphans the branches and worktrees of running agents (any branch created after that commit still contains the old line and would reintroduce it when merged), so it runs only in a quiet window with no live leases (task SEC-history-scrub) and never while agents are merging. The operator pushes, not an agent.

data.body: PARTLY ANSWERED 2026-10-31: question 1 (harness id) is decided as D-zcode-harness-id: rename glm to zcode, keep glm as an alias. STILL OPEN: (2) hook delivery under ZCode's workspace trust (user-level [REDACTED:path] with consent, project config plus an explicit trust step, or a plugin; default: user-level with consent); (3) scope 'all agents' = every feature the other harnesses have; (4) GLM models as their own model family for the cross-family reviewer rule; (5) allow installing zcode for the probe.

Operator 2026-10-31 (D-key-leak-handling): try to rewrite history before any push. PRECONDITIONS (check each, refuse otherwise): no live lease and no running agent merges (ddflow lanes shows none working; no pending merge-queue entry), the operator has said go, nothing has been pushed (git rev-list origin/main..main only). PROCEDURE: take a backup (git bundle of every ref to a path outside the repo and outside git); locate every occurrence across ALL refs and worktrees (git log --all -S with the key SHAPE pattern AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35}, never printing the value; also .ddflow/events working copies, .ddflow/blobs, .ddflow/backups, notes, research, docs); rewrite only the unpushed range with git filter-repo or filter-branch, replacing the key shape with [REDACTED:secret] inside the one event line, keeping the line valid JSON; then re-point or rebase every local ddflow/* branch and worktree onto the new main (branches created after 1deb26435 still contain the old line and would reintroduce it on merge: rebase them, or abandon and recreate); verify with git log --all -S, gitleaks over origin/main..main, ddflow replay (the event log must replay: the redacted line is a prompt text, not structure) and ddflow doctor; expire reflogs and gc the local object store to drop the old objects; record a ddflow note. The rewrite changes commit ids of every unpushed commit after 1deb26435: after it every agent worktree must be recreated; run it only when the queue is quiet. The operator pushes; an agent never pushes. If any precondition fails or the replay check fails, restore from the bundle and report.
data.title: Scrub the leaked key line from the unpushed history in a quiet window, before any push

## 2. Per-tool notes

**Claude Code**
- Best at: a harness primitives toolbox. It offers subagents, skills, hooks, plugins, MCP, memory, worktrees, `/review`, and Routines for cloud-scheduled, GitHub-triggered or API-triggered runs.
- ddflow could learn: (a) event-triggered routines (GitHub event or webhook to run a task), which are a first-class trigger type there; (b) plugin packaging, so a ddflow setup (rules, gates, agents) installs as one unit; (c) Agent Teams and subagent-defined tools.

**OpenAI Codex**
- Best at: a sandboxed cloud task that opens a PR, plus the Codex app as a "command center" for parallel agents. It also has Automations, `@codex review`, AGENTS.md and SKILL.md.
- ddflow could learn: read AGENTS.md and SKILL.md natively so one rule set is shared across harnesses. Also, an inbox for reviewing automation output (a review queue for scheduled findings).

**Kilo Code (and Roo / Cline)**
- Best at: modes with per-mode model and tool permissions, Orchestrator splitting work into subtasks, Memory Bank (markdown project context files), and cloud agents.
- ddflow could learn: custom modes as per-role tool allowlists and models. Memory Bank also suggests a human-readable "current context" file that is regenerated from the event log.

**Cursor / Windsurf**
- Best at: IDE integration, background agents, Bugbot for PR bugs, and path-scoped rules (`.cursor/rules` with globs).
- ddflow could learn: Bugbot-style one-click "fix this finding" flows from review findings to a task. Also glob-scoped rules that load only for matching files (ddflow rules already carry globs; confirm they are injected by file).

**GitHub Copilot and Spec Kit**
- Best at: the coding agent from an issue to a PR, running under Actions, with branch protection, CodeQL and Autofix. Spec Kit adds `/specify`, `/plan` and `/tasks` stages plus a constitution file and `/analyze` for cross-artifact consistency.
- ddflow could learn: a specify/plan stage in front of task creation, feeding acceptance criteria into the gates. Its `/analyze` is akin to the docs gate. A "constitution" maps to ddflow rules.

**Aider**
- Best at: a minimal git-native loop. It auto-commits each change, can run lint and tests after edits, and uses a repo map for context.
- ddflow could learn: a repo-map or symbol-index context pack for briefs. Auto-commit and undo semantics are also relevant.

**OpenHands / Devin / Amp**
- Best at: autonomous sessions in a VM with a browser and full environment. Devin adds Playbooks, Knowledge, a scheduled-session feature, ACU-based cost accounting and DeepWiki. Amp has threads shared with the team, plus an "oracle" second-model consult.
- ddflow could learn: shared and replayable session threads (a link a human can open). Playbooks are comparable to ddflow drivers or skills. ACU-style per-task budget with a stop limit. Amp's oracle resembles the rubber_duck gate, which supports the design.

**Gemini CLI / opencode / Goose / Mistral Vibe / Continue / Cody**
- Gemini CLI: GEMINI.md, MCP, extensions, headless mode, and GitHub Action integration. opencode: a client/server architecture with many providers, agents, and a plugin system. Goose: MCP-first, recipes (shareable parameterised workflows), and scheduling (unv.). Mistral Vibe: a CLI with AGENTS.md-style config and subagents (unv.). Continue: CI-run "checks" as markdown rules on PRs (unv.). Cody: code search and context (now largely folded into Amp).
- ddflow could learn: recipes, meaning parameterised, shareable workflow templates and headless/CI modes. Continue's agent checks as PR status checks are also worth copying. opencode's client/server split allows remote drive and a web UI.

**Taskmaster-AI / Backlog.md / OpenSpec / BMAD**
- Best at: lightweight task and spec files in-repo. Taskmaster adds PRD parsing, task expansion and complexity analysis. Backlog.md is markdown tasks with a TUI/web board. OpenSpec has proposal, delta and archive flow. BMAD has persona agents (analyst, PM, architect, dev, QA) and story files.
- ddflow could learn: PRD to tasks import with complexity scoring, and a kanban board that a human can read and edit. OpenSpec's change-delta archive is also worth studying. ddflow has `import` and a board view, so check parity rather than assume a gap.

**Claude-Flow / ruflo**
- Best at: swarm orchestration with topologies, a vector memory and many pre-built agents. It is more marketing than rigor (uncertain).
- ddflow could learn little; its enforced leases and gates are stronger. Worth watching how it does shared memory with embeddings.

**Conductor / Crystal / similar**
- Best at: a GUI for running several Claude Code or Codex sessions in separate worktrees, with diff review and one-click merge or PR.
- ddflow could learn: a live dashboard and diff view over lanes. These have no conflict prevention, which is ddflow's edge.

**CodeRabbit / Greptile / Qodo**
- Best at: PR review, with codebase-graph context (Greptile), learnings from past review comments (CodeRabbit), test generation (Qodo), and walkthrough summaries and sequence diagrams.
- ddflow could learn: a learnings loop where a human reaction to a review comment becomes a rule or lesson. Also a severity or confidence field on findings.

**Renovate / Dependabot**
- Best at: scheduled dependency PRs with grouping, auto-merge rules and a dashboard issue.
- ddflow could learn: a dependency-update source that files tasks in the queue, with grouping and a "dashboard" item.

**SonarQube / Semgrep / CodeQL**
- Best at: static analysis with quality gates, custom rule languages, SARIF output and PR decoration. Semgrep and CodeQL have autofix.
- ddflow could learn: SARIF ingestion (a finding becomes a bug record) and a quality-gate threshold. A bug_hunt gate that consumes SARIF would be cheap.

## 3. Candidate gaps for ddflow, ranked

Ranking is by how many tools have the capability, then by value. Some may already be partly implemented in ddflow; verify against the repo before filing.

1. **Event-triggered and durable scheduled runs.** Claude Code Routines, Codex Automations, Copilot (Actions), Devin, Renovate and Goose all have them (many tools, high value). ddflow has a cadence view but is a reminder, not an executor surviving restarts, per my read. Candidate: a scheduler or webhook trigger that files or claims tasks and runs a headless agent. This is the largest gap.
2. **PR review bot and PR-native integration.** Nearly every vendor (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor Bugbot, Copilot, Kilo, CodeRabbit, Devin) has one. ddflow has a PR integration mode, but no bot posting findings to PRs and no status check publishing gate results. Candidate: publish gate outcomes as GitHub check runs, and ingest PR review comments as findings.
3. **Cross-harness instruction files.** AGENTS.md, SKILL.md and GEMINI.md are now de facto standards (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini, Kilo, Taskmaster). Verify that ddflow reads and writes AGENTS.md and exports rules and skills in these formats.
4. **Shared, human-readable board and live dashboard.** Backlog.md, Crystal, Conductor, Devin, Amp and Copilot have one. ddflow has board and render views; a live web UI with diff review is the gap.
5. **Cost and budget enforcement.** Devin (ACUs), Kilo (per-request cost), Claude Code and Copilot (counters) all track cost. ddflow tracks metrics; gap is a hard per-task budget that stops or asks approval.
6. **Spec stage before tasks.** Spec Kit, OpenSpec, BMAD, Taskmaster and Kilo's Architect all have it. Candidate: spec or PRD artifact that the docs gate and acceptance criteria link to; verify what `import` already does.
7. **Static-analysis and dependency feeds.** SARIF from Semgrep, CodeQL or Sonar into bugs, and Renovate or Dependabot updates into tasks. Valuable and cheap.
8. **Learning from review feedback.** CodeRabbit learnings, Devin Knowledge, Cursor Memories. ddflow has lessons; the gap is automated capture from human PR comments or reverted agent edits.
9. **Packaged distribution.** Claude Code plugins, Goose recipes, Gemini extensions and Kilo marketplace bundle rules, agents and commands. Candidate: a ddflow pack that is installable in one step. The seed-pack work in the event log suggests this is underway.
10. **Per-mode model and tool permissions.** Kilo, Roo and Claude Code subagents have it. Check that ddflow's agent profiles restrict tools and models per role.
11. **Shareable session replay.** Devin, Amp and Claude Code transcripts have it. ddflow replays state but not conversation; a linkable thread view would help humans audit.
12. **Repo map or semantic index for briefs.** Aider, Cody, Greptile and Cursor use one. Lower priority since harnesses supply their own.

**ddflow's distinctive strengths, not found together elsewhere:** file-glob leases, mandatory cross-family review, a bug-to-regression-test requirement, and an append-only event log that supports replay. Do not trade these away for convenience features.

**Uncertain points:**
- Routines plan requirements.
- Whether Codex cloud automations have shipped.
- Copilot Memory status.
- Mistral Vibe and Continue details.
- All "?" and "unv." cells.

## Key framing

- **prek and pre-commit.** prek is a Rust, single-binary, drop-in reimplementation of pre-commit. It reads the same `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, also supports a native `prek.toml`, and runs several common hooks natively. Its recent releases added `check-commit-trailers`, `check-signed-commit` and `check-jsonc`. It is still pre-1.0 and some hook languages lack full parity. Default: write standard `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, which works with both, and prefer prek when it is installed.
- **Other hook runners.** lefthook (Go, runs commands in parallel) and husky (npm-only) are fine when the project already uses them. ddflow should detect an existing runner and not add a second one. Plain `.git/hooks` is not versioned, so ddflow should avoid it.
- **Core principle.** Hooks make a poor single enforcement point because `--no-verify` bypasses them. The same checks must run in CI as the real gate. The easiest way to guarantee that is to have both the hook and CI call one entry point, `pre-commit run --all-files` or `prek run --all-files`, or `ddflow` itself.

## (d) Stack detection and consent flow

**Detection by file (evidence, in order of reliability):**
- Lockfiles are strongest, because they prove the package manager and not only the language: `uv.lock`, `poetry.lock`, `Pipfile.lock`, `requirements*.txt`, `package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `yarn.lock`, `bun.lock`, `go.sum`, `Cargo.lock`, `Gemfile.lock`, `composer.lock`, `packages.lock.json`, `gradle.lockfile`.
- Manifests: `pyproject.toml`, `package.json`, `go.mod`, `Cargo.toml`, `pom.xml`, `build.gradle(.kts)`, `*.csproj`, `Gemfile`, `composer.json`, `flake.nix`.
- Tool config already present: `ruff.toml`, `[tool.ruff]`, `.eslintrc*`, `eslint.config.*`, `biome.json`, `.golangci.yml`, `deny.toml`, `.hadolint.yaml`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `lefthook.yml`, `.husky/`.
- Extras: `Dockerfile*`, `*.tf`, `.github/workflows/*.yml`, `*.sh`, `*.sql`, `*.md`.

**Detection hazards:**
- Ignore `node_modules`, `.venv`, `vendor` and other generated or vendored directories (use `git ls-files`, which respects `.gitignore`).
- Handle monorepos by detecting per sub-directory root and scoping tools with globs.
- Count a language only if it has real source files, not just a stray config.
- Record the evidence for each detection so the user can see why a tool is being proposed.

**Consent flow:**
1. Detect.
2. Propose (read-only dry run): show the exact config diff and the exact commands that would run.
3. The user accepts or rejects each proposal individually.
4. Write the config.
5. Run once in report-only mode to establish a baseline.
6. Enable enforcement only after the user confirms.

Rules for the flow:
- Never install anything silently, and never pin a tool at "latest" without a version.
- Respect existing tools: extend rather than replace.
- Record rejections so ddflow does not re-propose them.
- A tool that cannot run is `unavailable`, never `passed`.

## (f) CI and speed

**Speed**
- Split by stage with `default_stages` and `stages:`. Fast fixers and linters run at `pre-commit` on staged files only (ruff, biome, shellcheck, gitleaks `--staged`, hygiene hooks). Type checks, tests, audits and anything networked go to `pre-push` or CI.
- Set `fail_fast: false` for the full report, and `require_serial: false` for parallelism (prek parallelises by default).
- Cache: the hook environment cache (`[REDACTED:path]` or prek's cache) must be persisted in CI, keyed on the hash of the config file. Cache the uv, npm and cargo caches separately.
- Use `language: system` hooks, or `uv run`, for tools already in the project's lockfile. This avoids a second tool version, so the hook and CI agree.
- Run against `--from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD` in PR CI for speed, and run `--all-files` on a schedule and on main.
- Set a time budget, for example 5 seconds on commit, and measure it. Tools that exceed it move to a later stage.
- Skip hooks automatically on merge, rebase and amend where that is safe.

**CI**
- Run `pre-commit run --all-files` (or prek) as one job, then SCA, SAST and tests as separate parallel jobs.
- Pin actions by SHA, use least-privilege `permissions:`, and keep secret scans at `fetch-depth: 0`.
- Upload SARIF to code scanning from Semgrep, Trivy and zizmor.
- Use pre-commit.ci only as a convenience, not as the sole gate.

1. **Project-specific linters and policy.** Custom lint rules, architecture contracts, and a license policy (the allowed set).
2. **Build-tool-specific Java/Kotlin/.NET/C++ analysis.** Maven, Gradle, Bazel, CMake.
3. **Domain tools.** Data and notebooks (nbstripout, nbqa), ML artifacts and model files, game assets, firmware and embedded checks, mobile (Android lint, SwiftLint, Xcode), and proto or OpenAPI linting (buf, spectral).

## What an agent should return per proposal

For each tool the user could accept or reject:
- **Identity:** tool name, pinned version, and its source URL (with the date it was checked).
- **Evidence:** the project files that triggered the proposal (path, line or lockfile).
- **What it catches:** one line, with an example finding from this repo if a dry run was possible.
- **Dry-run result:** finding counts split into new and pre-existing, exit code, runtime in seconds, and the count of apparent false positives.
- **Proposed stage:** commit, push or CI, with the exact command.
- **Cost:** speed class, whether it needs the network, install method, and extra dependencies.
- **Overlap:** other proposed tools that would duplicate it, for example ruff `S` and bandit, or cargo-deny and cargo-audit.
- **Risk:** false-positive risk, maintenance status (last release, bus-factor notes), and supply-chain trust (publisher, signed releases, pinning ability).
- **Config diff:** the exact files to be created or changed.
- **Fallback:** what happens if the tool is unavailable (recorded `unavailable`).
- **Recommendation:** on by default, offer, or skip, with the reason.
- **Reversal:** how to remove it.
